title: Major Political Ideologies
hook: An ideology is a worldview about how society should be run — and a handful of them frame most political arguments you'll ever hear.
key_points: An ideology is a connected set of ideas about how society and government should be organized.
Liberalism centers individual rights, liberty, and limited, accountable government.
Conservatism stresses tradition, gradual change, and established institutions.
Socialism emphasizes equality and collective or public provision; other families include nationalism and green thought.
content_html: A political ideology is a connected set of ideas about how society and government ought to be organized — what counts as a good society, what government is for, and how change should happen. Ideologies matter because they turn scattered opinions into coherent worldviews, giving people and parties a consistent lens for judging issues they have never specifically considered. A few broad families frame most political debate.
extra_html: Liberalism places the individual at the center: it prizes personal liberty, rights, and equality before the law, and favors government that is limited, accountable, and constrained by those rights. Conservatism emphasizes continuity — respect for tradition, established institutions, and social order, with a preference for gradual reform over radical change, on the view that inherited arrangements often encode hard-won wisdom. Socialism foregrounds equality and solidarity, favoring collective or public provision and a more active role for the state in distributing resources, with a long internal range from democratic socialism to more radical forms. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that other major families sit alongside these, including nationalism (which centers the nation and its identity), and green or environmentalist thought (which centers ecological sustainability). Real parties usually blend several strands rather than embodying one in pure form, and the same label can mean different things in different countries.

related.title: The Left–Right Spectrum
related.hook: "Left" and "right" are political shorthand the whole world uses — but they began as nothing more than which side of a room people sat on.

related.title: Political Parties & Party Systems
related.hook: Parties are how scattered voters become an organized choice. Whether a country has two big ones or a dozen shapes how its whole politics feels.

related.title: Populism
related.hook: Populism isn't a single program — it's a style that splits society into two camps: a virtuous 'people' against a corrupt 'elite,' with the populist speaking for the people.

flashcards.prompt: Which idea is most central to classical liberalism?

choices.text: Individual rights, liberty, and limited, accountable government
Hereditary rule by a single family

flashcards.explanation_html: Liberalism centers individual freedom and rights, with government limited and accountable rather than all-controlling.

choices.text: Tradition, established institutions, and gradual rather than radical change

flashcards.explanation_html: Conservatism values continuity, established institutions, and incremental reform over abrupt transformation.
